Because retros are required by the CI tooling itself, regardless of team choice
Because the bug can't actually be fixed without a retro happening first
Because it guarantees an identical bug will never occur again anywhere in the codebase
items.explanation: L3's Checkpoint ties the retro's value directly back to L1: absorbing a gap silently, even after fixing it, teaches the team the same 'somebody else's problem' lesson QA's absence originally revealed.
items.reference:
🐛 Null-handling bug, uncovered branch
⏱️ 30-minute retro, scaled to size — not skipped, not overblown
📝 Strategy table gets a new row as a direct result

Why: treating even a small regression seriously is what keeps the gate meaning something months later.

items.prompt: Per L3's closing extension question, what does the unit ask the reader to consider about scaling this approach to a 200-person org?
choices: Whether a blocking CI gate still works the same way across dozens of independently-deploying services, or whether the strategy-table step needs to happen at a different level entirely
Whether QA should be reinstated once headcount exceeds 50 people
Whether the same six-week timeline would simply repeat unchanged at any scale
The question only concerns hiring more staff engineers, per L3
items.explanation: L3's first extension question specifically asks whether a single-team mechanism (blocking gate, one standards meeting) still holds at org scale with many independently-deploying services, or whether the strategy decision needs a different organizational level.
items.reference:
🏢 8-person team → 200-person org: does the mechanism still hold?
👔 IC pushback vs. director pushback: same negotiation, or different?

Why: the worked example is one case, not the whole territory — the mechanism's limits are worth testing on purpose.
